ShortRequest.paper, in openapi-public.json today: "Per-trade paper override —
honoured only on the spot-bear fallback (cards without an EVCDX token); perps
are always real-ledger". So a short on a card that has an EVCDX token opens a
real-ledger position while the request said paper, and the caller has no
documented way to tell which cards those are before ordering.
reports.description:
This is the sharpest form of the family that #80 was about, and we are filing
it separately because #80 asked whether a caller CAN state the book — which
you closed properly, and we have sent the pass. This asks whether stating it
is enough.
An ignored explicit instruction is worse than an undocumented default. With a
default, a careful caller learns the rule once and complies. Here the caller
did everything right: it read the schema, it sent the canonical control, it
asked for the one thing that guarantees no real money moves — and on some
cards it gets a real perp. It cannot even choose to avoid those cards, because
we could find no published field saying which cards carry an EVCDX token.
We are not asking for paper perps. If the perp ledger cannot be simulated, the
safe behaviour is the one you already chose for the CLOB an hour ago: refuse.
A 400 saying "paper is not available for perp shorts on this card" costs the
caller one branch and cannot cost it money. Silently downgrading paper=true to
a real position is the case that can.
Credit where it is due: we only found this because your new description says
so plainly. The previous text did not, and the behaviour was the same.

reports.actual_behavior:
It answers 200 with total 0 under every query shape we tried — bare, with
limit, with offset, with include_paper, with mode=paper, with type=all — while
GET /api/v1/portfolio/summary on the same account in the same minute reports
total_predictions 142 and total_volume 3582.15, and GET /api/v1/event-
cards/positions lists 39 positions. One of those positions was opened eleven
minutes earlier by the same API key doing the reading.
reports.description:
Two readings fit what we can see from outside, and we cannot tell them apart,
so we are reporting both rather than guessing.
Either the endpoint is blind to this account's activity, or it is scoped to an
identity our API key is not. The second is not speculation: the sibling GET
/api/v1/swap/history answers 401 "Valid JWT token required" for the same key,
so per-identity scoping demonstrably exists on this part of the API. If
/api/v1/trades is JWT-scoped by design, then it is returning 200 and an empty
list where it means "not your identity" — which an agent reads as "you have
never traded".
Why we think it is worth your time rather than a curiosity: /build tells an
agent to save the api_key and send it as X-API-Key on every call, and then to
trade. An agent that cannot read back its own fills cannot reconcile a
position, cannot compute its own P&L, and cannot tell a retry from a duplicate
order. This is the endpoint anyone reaches for first — it is called "trade
history" and there is no second one.
We are not claiming a number. We do not know how many trades you should report
for this account; the products may well be counted differently. What cannot
both be true is zero trades and 142 predictions on the same account in the
same minute.
If the answer is scoping, the cheapest fix is documentation plus a status: say
in llms.txt which identity and which products it covers, and answer 401 rather
than an empty 200 when the caller is not the identity it serves. An empty 200
is indistinguishable from a true empty history, and that is the part that
misleads.

reports.actual_behavior:
Neither holds. The paper/live control is named three different ways across
four order endpoints and the defaults diverge: omitting it on an event-card
trade or a bot clone inherits user.simulation_mode, while omitting `mode` on
an exchange order is documented as "live". The CLOB order schema has no such
field at all. And user.simulation_mode, the setting two of those resolve
against, appears three times in openapi-public.json — every occurrence prose
inside a request body. No documented response returns it and llms.txt does not
mention it.
reports.description:
We are not reporting that the modes are wired wrongly. Each endpoint probably
does exactly what its own description says. The defect is that an autonomous
caller cannot act on them safely, and /build is an invitation to autonomous
callers specifically.
The concrete failure: an agent sets itself to paper, writes one helper that
omits the optional flag because omitting it worked against the event-card
endpoint, and then places a REAL order the first time that helper is pointed
at the exchange. Nothing in the response to any prior call would have warned
it, because the setting it thought it was inheriting is not published anywhere
it can read.
We got this wrong ourselves today, which is why we think it is worth your
time. Reading an unauthenticated fetch of /aci-challenge, we saw "PAPER
TRADING MODE" and concluded our own account was in paper. It is live, with
real USDC in it. The badge in the logged-in UI says so plainly — the API says
nothing at all, and we had no way to check without the browser.
Two changes would close it, and they are independent: publish the effective
mode on a read an agent already makes (portfolio/summary or /mcp/v1/agents/me
would both be natural), and make the four order endpoints agree on one field
name and one default. If you would rather not change the exchange default,
saying so in the field description — "unlike the event-card endpoints, this
does not inherit simulation_mode" — would remove most of the risk on its own.

Neither. The rows carry six different headline_period values and
headline_return_pct is reported against whichever of them the row uses, so the
column cannot be sorted. ?period=30d is accepted and ignored. An agent that
ranks by headline_return_pct, which is the only return figure on the row,

reports.description:
We are not reporting the leaderboard's numbers as wrong. Each row's figure
looks right for its own period; the defect is that the recipe asks for a
ranking the response cannot express, and nothing on the row warns the caller.
The reason we are filing this at medium rather than as documentation: the next
clause of the same sentence is "fund it with $50, go live". The incomparable
number is the one a funding decision rests on, and an agent has no way to
notice — headline_return_pct is a single numeric column and sorting it is the
obvious thing to do with a leaderboard.
Any of three fixes would close it, and the choice is yours: accept ?period and
filter, publish a per-period return alongside the headline, or change the
recipe to name the ranking the data actually supports. If you take the third,
we would suggest the recipe say which field to rank on, since "best" over a
mixed-period table is the ambiguity itself.
Two of the sixteen rows do carry "30 days", so an agent could in principle
filter client-side — but only by string-matching a display label, and it would
be choosing from two rows while believing it chose from sixteen.
